THE THREE ARMS, each asserting EXACT code AND layer against the production reader readCurrentActiveGraph, and each declaring `arranged` so the suite's series check (`expected.layer === arranged`) proves the fixture reached the layer it was built for:
- BEFORE  a real DRAFT-only history driven through reduceGraphRevision, committed, never activated -> ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT @ ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION. Chose a DRAFT history over an empty store on purpose: an empty store and an unactivated one must both refuse, and only the second shows the lifecycle filter doing the refusing.
- AFTER   a revision driven all the way to ACTIVE and committed, whose body was never recorded -> ACTIVE_GRAPH_BODY_UNAVAILABLE @ ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION, sourceLayer GRAPH_BODY_RECORD, sourceCode GRAPH_BODY_ABSENT.
- RACE    two ACTIVE revisions with real bodies committed from TWO SEPARATE CONNECTIONS to the same store file, then both connections read concurrently -> both sides ACTIVE_GRAPH_SPLIT_BRAIN @ ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION, maxAdmitted 0. Neither reader may resolve a split brain; "the later one wins" would be a resolution dressed as a read.
That covers the layer's entire published vocabulary (ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION_CODES, all three).

PLAN CORRECTION on the layer subtlety. The plan warned that active-graph-projection.ts:203 "refuses ACTIVE_GRAPH_BODY_UNAVAILABLE under GRAPH_BODY_RECORD_LAYER, not under its own". Reading the code: refuse() ALWAYS sets layer: ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION_LAYER; the body-record layer arrives in the separate sourceLayer field. An arm asserting layer: GRAPH_BODY_RECORD for that code would have been asserting a combination production never emits — the opposite error the warning intended to prevent. Recorded here because the same warning will otherwise be re-read at QA time.

BEYOND THE THREE ARMS, because a {code, layer} case structurally cannot carry these:
- An ACCEPTED CONTROL through the same production reader over the whole lawful path (ACTIVE revision + its body): asserts ok true, revisionId, graphContentHash and snapshotIdentity, and that snapshotIdentity is NOT the content hash. Without it, a projection that refused everything would satisfy every arm above.
- A property block pinning layer (who answered) against sourceLayer (who refused): all four refusals carry layer ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION; exactly one is wrapped and carries sourceLayer GRAPH_BODY_RECORD + sourceCode GRAPH_BODY_ABSENT; the other three carry null in both. Exactly-one, not at-least-one — zero would make the source assertions vacuous.
- A capture-count property (5 proofs: BEFORE, AFTER, RACE x2, CONTROL) so a group that silently generated nothing cannot leave the rest quantified over an empty list.

TWO WHOLE-SLICE INVARIANTS EXTENDED, not weakened. The new control is an admission by design, so "never admits an activation" (admittedTotal === allowed + admittedControls) and "collected an outcome from every case" (CASES + RACES*2 + controls) both had to learn about it. The admission count is READ OFF production's returned value via isAdmitted(), never hard-coded: a control that had silently refused still reddens.

Rail 1 is absolute here: own only `tests/security/**` and do NOT modify `apps/daemon/src/planning/**` or `apps/daemon/src/projections/**` — the readers are other tasks' deliverables. THE THREE ARMS, each pinning exact code AND layer against the production readers putGraphBody/readGraphBody, each declaring `arranged` so the series check holds:
- BEFORE  a body never recorded, read before any write -> GRAPH_BODY_ABSENT @ GRAPH_BODY_RECORD, sourceLayer null. Absence must not collapse into corruption; one code for both would hide a lost row.
- AFTER   after a LAWFUL body landed through the real writer, canonical codec bytes are planted under a RIVAL content's key -> GRAPH_BODY_IDENTITY_MISMATCH @ GRAPH_BODY_RECORD, sourceLayer null. The decoder cannot catch this on its own — those bytes are perfectly self-consistent — so only the key-versus-digest check can answer.
- RACE    two SEPARATE CONNECTIONS racing putGraphBody with a hand-serialised body (real hash, real content, non-codec bytes) -> both refused GRAPH_BODY_NOT_ENCODED @ GRAPH_BODY_RECORD, maxAdmitted 0, AND durableAdmissions reads the durable row count back as 0. A returned refusal is not evidence nothing was written; the defect worth catching is a custodian that says no to both callers while a forged body lands.
All three of the record's own frozen codes are exercised, asserted as a set so the family property below cannot be satisfied by one code repeated.

THE UNION THE PLAN FLAGGED, made observable. GraphBodyRefusal.code is GraphBodyRecordCode | GraphContentIssueCode. Two properties pin which family answered:
- every hostile arm's code is a member of production's own frozen GRAPH_BODY_RECORD_CODES and carries sourceLayer null;
- a PASSTHROUGH positive control (one drifted character inside otherwise canonical bytes) is refused by the CODEC and passed through: layer still GRAPH_BODY_RECORD, sourceLayer NOT null, and its code is NOT in GRAPH_BODY_RECORD_CODES. Without that control, "every refusal came from the own vocabulary" would be a property nothing could break — the codec family would look unreachable rather than merely unused.
Plus an ACCEPTED control: bytes written by the real writer and read back by the real reader (ok, graphContentHash, snapshotIdentity, and bytes still a Uint8Array — the record stores codec output verbatim and never re-serialises).

TWO DECLARED DEVIATIONS, both inside tests/security/**, neither touching apps/**:

1. THE PLANTED ROW. Production is content-addressed: putGraphBody derives the aggregate key from the bytes' own hash, so a misfiled or corrupt row is UNREACHABLE through the writer. A read-side identity check no fixture can reach is an unguarded check, so the AFTER arm and the passthrough control commit a body row directly, with the codec's own bytes; only the key they are filed under, or one drifted character inside them, is hostile. Declared in the module header, not hidden. Rail 1 holds — the readers are untouched.

2. THE RATCHET NEEDED REGISTERING. completeness.security.ts enumerates the axis case TABLES by import; it does not scan the lane for scheduler-activation. My arms live in a new sibling module, so the ratchet read them as six uncovered roster rows ("ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION_LAYER ... has no BEFORE case", etc.) even with the slice fully green. That is +8/-2 in another task's file (task-3b1cbdf9's ratchet) but inside this task's owned tests/security/** scope, and it is the only way a sibling table can be seen. The alternative — smuggling planning-graph arms into SCHEDULER_DECISION_CASES so the existing import picked them up — would have been a lie about what that table holds.
